newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma still cracking down on democracy - Suu Kyi.
newsitem.headline: Burma still cracking down on democracy - Suu Kyi.

text.p: Pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi said on Friday Burma's military regime was still cracking down on the country's democracy movement as questions grow over whether Rangoon should be allowed into a key regional forum.

Suu Kyi told reporters the military government had detained up to seven youth members of her National League for Democracy (NLD) party in the past week for questioning about an October 23 student protest.
She said at least two of them had been released after being interrogated "very severely" during their detention.

Here statement came as some members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) appeared to be leaning toward delaying Burma's membership in the organisation following protests over the regime's suppression of democracy.
Burma has been granted observer status to ASEAN and is seeking full membership at its next formal meeting in July.
Foreign Minister Ohn Gyaw said on Friday he was confident Burma would be accepted as a full member.
"By virtue of the fact that you have observer status it is just a matter of time. Sooner or later you will be integrated into ASEAN," he told a monthly news conference.
A senior ASEAN delegation was due to arrive in Burma on Saturday for a week-long examination of Rangoon's preparations for entry into the bloc.

Some of ASEAN's Western trading partners oppose Burma's entry into the forum because of the poor human rights record of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) and its refusal to hold talks with Suu Kyi's democracy movement.
Political analysts said Rangoon's application for full ASEAN membership was likely to be side-stepped at the July meeting, possibly on economic grounds.

"It is premature to talk about a reversal in policy, but I think ASEAN is looking for an escape clause -- a reason to delay Burma's membership," said Ishtiaq Hossain, a senior lecturer in political science at the National University of Singapore.
But senior Defence Ministry official Colonel Kyaw Thein said on Friday the SLORC was taking steps to improve relations with Nobel Peace laureate Suu Kyi and the NLD.
"Both sides may be trying to improve the situation (and) their understanding of each other," he told reporters after the news conference.
He said Kyi Maung, a top aide to Suu Kyi and duputy NLD chairman, was detained on October 23 for questioning, partly to give the SLORC an understanding of the pro-democracy party's current attitude.
"We wanted to have a clearer picture of what we are thinking about the NLD and concerning the current situation," he said.

Kyi Maung, who was released on Monday, told Reuters on Friday he had tried to explain the NLD's desire to carry on its duties as any registered party would. He said he complained over how SLORC treated the NLD.
"I told them the key was contact," he said. "I think they are learning. They listened to what I had to say."

Suu Kyi -- daughter of national hero Aung San, who led Burma to the brink of independence from British colonial rule before his assassination in 1947 -- would not say if relations with the SLORC were gradually warming.
But she said she welcomed any chance to hold talks with the government.

Suu Kyi said she also was determined to resume her regular weekend rallies as soon as possible. For the past five weekends, the SLORC has prevented her from giving speeches to supporters outside her gates by blocking access to the road past her home.
Kyaw Thein at the Defence Ministry hinted that Suu Kyi may be allowed to resume the weekend speeches if she agreed to hold them inside the gates of her compound.
But Suu Kyi said she had no plans to move the talks inside.
"We stand by our policy that as long as people are prepared to come, we shall hold rallies outside the gates," she said. "We have no plans to hold them inside the compound."
Suu Kyi also welcomed recent sanctions by the European Union that bar visas to SLORC members and their families and suspends high-level EU visits to Burma.
